mechaber.en:
One whose animal regularly enters another person's field, and butchers' animals that cause damage. It contains two seifim.
If a person's animal regularly enters another's field and damages it, the field owner may warn the animal's owner to guard it, and the owner must do so. If he fails to guard it and it causes damage, he must pay. He cannot tell the field owner, 'Fence your field so that my animal cannot enter.'

Fenced. The owners are obligated to guard their animals so they do not cause damage. This is comparable to an animal eating from inside a shop, as stated in siman 391, seif 9, and the owner cannot say, "You should have closed your shop." The Tur, however, writes that Rabbenu Tam and the Rosh disagree and hold that this is not comparable to eating from inside a shop. So writes the Sema. The Shach likewise rules that if the landowner did not fence his property and an animal entered and ate, the animal's owner is exempt. The Torah's liability for tooth "in another's field" applies only where the animal burrowed under the fence or where the fence fell at night. He discusses this at length and concludes that since Halachot Gedolot, Rabbenu Chananel, Raavan, the Rosh, and the Tur all hold the owner exempt, that is the law. The traditions of Halachot Gedolot and Rabbenu Chananel are received from the Gemara, and I have also demonstrated that their reasoning is primary. Shach.

The wording of the Tur in the name of Ri, from the incident involving the goats of Bei Tarbu, as Rabbi Yosef said to Abaye, Bava Metzia chapter 2, 53b.
In my humble opinion this requires study. According to Rosh, the owner can say, 'Fence your field,' following Rabbenu Chananel, as the Tur writes immediately below. According to Tosafot, who bring proof from an animal eating inside shops, it appears the animal owner must pay even without prior warning. Raavad likewise writes this, and the Maggid Mishneh in chapter 5 of Hilkhot Nizkei Mamon writes in the name of most commentators that payment is due even without warning. In my humble opinion, warning serves only to require removal of the damaging animal. Even if the owner pays the damage, the victim should not be forced repeatedly to litigate, and sometimes a person may be unable to do so, as Tosafot write concerning the goats of the marketplace. Ritva and the Ramah, cited by Nimukei Yosef, likewise hold that the owners are placed under ban until they remove the danger.
Because the halachah does not follow Abaye's response to Rav Yosef. Rif writes that it was merely a deflection, and Tosafot likewise say Abaye was evading the matter because he did not wish to go there.

חננאל וראב"ן והרא"ש וטור סוברים דפטור הכי נקטינן דכבר נודע שדברי ה"ג ור"ח דברי קבלה הם מהש"ס ובפרט שהוכחתי שדבריהם עיקר:
siftei_kohen.en: He must pay for its damage and cannot, etc. Beit Yosef attributes this rule to Rambam in Hilchot Nizkei Mamon, chapter 5, but I searched the Rambam and found no such statement. Rambam’s ruling that an owner pays when his animal damages other fields proves nothing, for the verse itself speaks of grazing in another field, and the Gemara limits liability to a case where the owner fenced the animal in and it burrowed out, or the fence fell at night. Beit Yosef’s assertion that the Rosh is inconclusive is also surprising, since the Rosh ultimately cites Rabbeinu Chananel and rejects Tosafot, so the Tur correctly states that the Rosh concludes like Rabbeinu Chananel. Maharshal rejects Rabbeinu Chananel because shepherds are presumed robbers and disqualified from testimony for failing to guard against entry into other fields. He argues that if every landowner had to fence his field, all fields would ordinarily be fenced. I do not agree. Even if the animal’s owner is exempt where the field was unfenced, people generally do not fence all fields, because damage by stray animals is uncommon and one cannot fence the entire world. Shepherds are disqualified because they intentionally graze in others’ fields. Nor may we decide against Abaye merely because Rav Yosef was his teacher. From Abaye and Rava onward, the law generally follows the later authority, and the Gemara’s anonymous discussion appears to accept Abaye’s answer that liability for tooth applies where the animal burrowed through or the wall fell at night. Halachot Gedolot and Raavan explicitly rule like Abaye. Since Halachot Gedolot, Rabbeinu Chananel, Raavan, the Rosh, and the Tur all rule that the owner is exempt where the field was not fenced, that is the practical ruling, especially since their reading of the sugya is primary.
